title: Reflection
subtitle: Java Teaching Studio · Live Session Lecture

title: Overview
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Reflection is a powerful and advanced feature of Java that allows a program to **examine and modify itself at runtime**.
With reflection, you can look inside any class, discover its methods, fields, and constructors, and even invoke them — all while the program is running, without knowing the class at compile time.

title: Real-World Analogy
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Imagine a doctor performing an X-ray on a patient.
The patient doesn't need to do anything differently.
The X-ray machine (reflection) looks *inside* the body (class) and reveals its internal structure — bones, organs, sizes — without the patient's active cooperation.
The doctor can then act on what they find.
Reflection does the same for Java classes. It peeks inside them at runtime and exposes their internal structure.

title: What Reflection Can Do
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
| Capability | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| Inspect a class | Get class name, modifier, interfaces implemented |
| Inspect methods | Get method names, return types, parameters, modifiers |
| Inspect fields | Get field names, types, modifiers |
| Inspect constructors | Get constructor parameters and modifiers |
| **Invoke methods** | Call any method (including private) at runtime |
| **Change field values** | Set any field (including private) at runtime |
| **Create objects** | Call any constructor (including private) at runtime |

title: What is the `Class` Class?
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Before you can reflect anything, you need to understand `java.lang.Class`. This is a special class whose name is literally `Class` — and it is the **entry point** for all reflection.

title: Who Creates Class Objects?
subtitle: The JVM creates them — not you.
bullets: **The JVM creates them — not you.**

When the JVM loads a class (e.g., `Bird`), it:
1.
Reads the compiled `.class` bytecode file.
Creates an instance of `java.lang.Class` internally.
Populates that `Class` instance with metadata about `Bird`.

title: Method 1 — `Class.forName(String className)`
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Pass the fully qualified class name as a `String`. This is useful when you **don't have the class available at compile time** (the most dynamic approach).

title: Method 2 — `.class` Literal
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: If you have access to the class type at compile time, use the `.class` literal directly on the class name. This is the safest and most readable approach.
No exception handling required — this is resolved at compile time.

title: Method 3 — `object.getClass()`
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: If you already have an **instance** of the class, call `getClass()` on it. This is inherited from `java.lang.Object`, so every Java object has this method.
This is useful when you receive an object of unknown type and want to inspect it dynamically.
code:
Eagle eagle = new Eagle();
Class<?> eagleClass = eagle.getClass();

title: Side-by-Side Comparison
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: | Method | Syntax | Compile-time class needed?
| Exception?

| Best Used When |
|--------|--------|---------------------------|-----------|----------------|
| `Class.forName()` | `Class.forName("Eagle")` | ❌ No — string only | ✅ Yes — `ClassNotFoundException` | Class name known only at runtime (plugins, frameworks) |
| `.class` literal | `Eagle.class` | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | Class known at compile time |
| `getClass()` | `obj.getClass()` | ✅ Yes (object exists) | ❌ No | You already have an instance |

title: getMethods() vs getDeclaredMethods()
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
| Feature | `getMethods()` | `getDeclaredMethods()` |
|---------|---------------|----------------------|
| Access scope | `public` only | All — `public` + `private` + `protected` + default |
| Inherited methods?

| ✅ Yes — includes `Object` methods | ❌ No — current class only |
| Private methods?

| ❌ No | ✅ Yes |
| Use when | You want all publicly accessible behavior | You want to inspect exactly what this class defines |

title: Background — What is Singleton?
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: The **Singleton pattern** ensures that only **one instance** of a class ever exists.

It is implemented using:
1.

A `private` constructor (prevents external instantiation via `new`)
2.
A `static` method that controls access to the single instance

title: The Rule
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
| Method | Scope | Access Level Returned |
|--------|-------|----------------------|
| `getFields()` | Class + all superclasses | `public` only |
| `getDeclaredFields()` | This class only | `public` + `private` + `protected` + default |
| `getMethods()` | Class + all superclasses | `public` only |
| `getDeclaredMethods()` | This class only | All access levels |
| `getConstructors()` | This class only | `public` only |
| `getDeclaredConstructors()` | This class only | All access levels |

subtitle: Conceptual Details

title: Reason 1 — It Breaks Encapsulation
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Object-oriented programming is built on the principle of **encapsulation**: private members are private for a reason.
They represent internal implementation details that other classes should not access or modify.
Reflection completely bypasses this:

title: Reason 2 — It is Slow
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Reflection works at **runtime** by doing name-based lookups.

Every time you call `getMethod("fly")`, the JVM must:
1.
Search through the class's method list by string comparison.
Resolve parameter types.

title: Reason 3 — It Defeats IDE and Compiler Safety
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: The IDE cannot check if `"fly"` actually exists.
The compiler cannot catch typos.
Errors only surface at runtime as `NoSuchMethodException`.
code:
// Typo — compiler is silent, IDE is silent, crashes at runtime:
Method m = Eagle.class.getDeclaredMethod("fyl");  // NoSuchMethodException at runtime

title: Summary of Disadvantages
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
| Disadvantage | Impact |
|-------------|--------|
| Breaks encapsulation | Private members can be accessed/modified by anyone |
| Runtime performance | 10–100x slower than direct access |
| No compile-time safety | Typos in method/field names only fail at runtime |
| Breaks Singleton | Private constructors can be invoked |
| Complexity | Code is harder to read, debug, and maintain |

title: Most Frequently Asked Questions
subtitle: Q1: What is Java Reflection?
bullets: **Q1: What is Java Reflection?**
A: Java Reflection is an API (`java.lang.reflect`) that allows a program to inspect and manipulate the structure of classes, methods, fields, and constructors at runtime — even private ones.
It is typically used by frameworks like Spring, Hibernate, and JUnit.
**Q2: What is the `Class` class in Java?**
A: `java.lang.Class` is a class whose instances represent classes and interfaces at runtime.
